doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Fairbanks arts festival, Chris Calloway and Grover Sales, return East in 1989
summary: At the Fairbanks summer arts festival Gates takes Chris Calloway's cabaret class, meets Grover Sales, and is encouraged to move to New York, where he meets and sits in with heroes.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: performing headliners, one was Sarah Vaughan and one was Steve Allen. Yeah. I said wow. And it was a two week festival. And it wasn’t just performances. It was workshops that you could attend. And these workshops were from square dancing to photography to charcoal drawing to classical violin, singing, dancing, you name it. Arts festival. And they had to two week cabaret class. Not my thing but the instructor was a woman by the name of Chris Calloway. Cab’s daughter. Well that was enough for me to sign up. Cab Calloway’s daughter is teaching a cabaret class? Wow. And it was going to be a piano player and a bass player and you’d have to audition, and if you got in you’d take these classes. Two hours a day for two weeks. And then a performance at the end of it. So I signed up. You know I’m in Fairbanks during the summer to have a good time. And after about the third or fourth class, I’m sitting in the back and there’s a gentleman sitting back there with a clip board, and he’s writing, and I thought he was a participant in the class. So we struck up a conversation and it turned out that he was a writer from San Francisco who was up there writing about this festival. And his name was Grover Sales. Come to find out, he’s an educator, an author, he wrote Jazz: America’s Classical Music, he wrote a Charlie Parker biography, he had the most extensive interviews with Thelonious Monk, he taught at one of the big colleges in San Francisco, I can’t remember the name off hand but he was this very interesting, very hip guy. He was Dizzy Gillespie’s road manager in the late 1950s, so when I found out that I mean I was just pumping him and he was happy to tell me all these stories. And he heard me sing a couple of times and he said to me, “Where are you from?” I said, “I live here in Fairbanks.” He said, “That’s not what I asked you, where are you from?” I said, “Connecticut.” He said, “Yeah.” He said, “You know what you do is very different than what is going on here.” I said, “Yeah, I know but I’m coming to learn something and I never really got to do this in the way that they’re explaining it so I’m just having a good time.” And they had like sixty instructors from all over the world. Some were classical. Fred Budda, a famous drummer who has now passed, from Boston. There were a couple of Boston guys, there were some San Francisco guys, New York guys, and my take on the music was a little different than the rest of the cabaret singers, and they encouraged me. They said, “You know you’ve got your own sound.” One of them said to me, “What are you doing up here, man, you’ll never get heard up here.” I said, “I’m not trying to get heard, I live up here. I work up here.” And they couldn’t understand like why. Why would you want to live up here? Well because it’s beautiful. It gets a little cool in the winter, and a little dark, but I didn’t come up here for the weather, I came up here for an adventure and it just kind of kept going. And I was trying to make money. You know I was just a po’ boy from Bridgeport. So I was trying to make what they used to call a grub stake. You know? And after a while I got encouraged from these people. The music felt so good. I was on a bandstand with © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

people who really could play, as opposed to people who couldn’t play that good. That’s who I was usually playing with. And it felt good. And I thought you know I’m getting kind of tired of bouncing around on a piece of equipment, maybe I’ll go back to the East Coast. I’ll go to New York City and I’ll see if I can make a little noise. Because these people encouraged me. And in my mind, and I’ve said this to a few people and I’m going to say it again although I don’t have rehearsed lines, but I knew that — I went back to Connecticut in ’89. I knew that Thelonious Monk and Charlie Parker had already passed but I thought I might run into them in New York. Well when I got there they were going baby, but I did get to meet some people who I was knocked out to meet like Max Roach and Lou Donaldson and Mose Allison and I got to work with Walter Bishop Junior and Lou and I met guys that were my age but they were heavy hitters: Jon Faddis, Richie Cole, and I got to interact with them and talk to them and sit in with them and they encouraged me. And Buddy Tate I mentioned. Bill Finnegan, Eddie Bert, people that you interviewed that I watched the interviews and listened. I just felt like wow, I was inspired by them and by being able to partake in what they were doing. But it wasn’t easy.
